newsitem.title: JAPAN: Hashimoto asks Okinawa's help on U.S. bases.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto asks Okinawa's help on U.S. bases.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto asked Okinawa Governor Masahide Ota for help on Thursday in winning over municipalities opposing the relocation of a U.S. Marine Corps air base, a prefectural spokesman said.

Hashimoto's meeting with Ota in Naha, the capital of Okinawa, followed Monday's key U.S.-Japan agreement to streamline U.S. bases on Okinawa, the island which hosts more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan.
Hashimoto was in Okinawa to attend a one-day conference of Asian welfare ministers.

A sticking point in the agreement, to cut back a fifth of the land now taken up by the U.S. military on Okinawa, is the relocation of the Futenma Air Station in southern Okinawa to an offshore base somewhere on the east coast of the island.

The mayor of Nago, the most likely location of the new base, said he opposed the move and was joined by a chorus of other mayors, scholars and activists after Monday's deal was announced by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry and other U.S. and Japanese officials in Tokyo.
"I need the cooperation of Okinawa prefecture over the final Okinawa report," the spokesman quoted Hashimoto as telling Ota. The spokesman said Hashimoto was speaking about Futenma.

Ota replied that he would start discussions with the mayors only if they asked him for advice. "The important thing is to clearly state when the United States would be leaving Futenma," Ota told Hashimoto.
Until three months ago, Ota led a campaign against the central government to block the renewal of contracts for land used by U.S. bases.
Ota dropped the campaign after Tokyo repeatedly apologised for having done nothing to lessen Okinawa's burden and promised moves to prop up the sagging island economy.

The bitter row flared up in September 1995 after the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen, which put the spotlight on the lopsided concentration of U.S. bases on Okinawa. The three are serving up to 10 years in jail.
